newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Maize and mud huts hide Zairean copper wealth.
newsitem.headline: Maize and mud huts hide Zairean copper wealth.

text.p: No one lived at Tenke-Fungurume in the bush of south Zaire until copper was found some 40 years ago. Now 30,000 people call it home, but not an ounce of the metal has yet been mined.
The land, flat but dotted with small ridges, is still covered with trees, long grass and maize fields that hide what are believed to be the world's richest copper and cobalt reserves below the soil.
Here and there, a scar on a hillside shows where geologists drilled to probe the riches and where investors say the world's biggest open-cast copper mine will soon start to take shape.

Tenke-Fungurume Mining Corp., a joint venture between state-owned Gecamines and Canada's Consolidated Eurocan Ventures Ltd., says it is ploughing a quarter of a billion dollars into the site to get it going by the year 2000.

Chairman Ted Webb exudes optimism, saying Zaire's six-month-old war is a passing storm that won't affect what is the biggest planned investment in the central African state since things started to go wrong here in the 1970s.
"We don't see any immediate threats and continue to plan on that basis. We will fly in drill rigs and workers on April 18 as planned," he said by telephone from his London base.
However, earlier attempts to mine here have come undone.
Through the weeds you can just see the shells of houses that were built for a workforce that never got to work.
Some locals say Tenke is a doomed place, destined to thwart anyone who comes to exploit it.
First came the private company Union Miniere, which earmarked the site for development in the 1960s, but was nationalised as Gecamines by President Mobutu Sese Seko.
He handed over the concession to a foreign consortium, led by Anglo American Corp. of South Africa.
They invested $300 million but lost it all when they abandoned the project in 1978 due to political risk.

The trigger for their overnight departure was the massacre of Belgian families living in the nearby copper town of Kolwezi in one of several attempts by the mineral-rich Shaba province to secede from Zaire and keep more of its wealth for itself.
Since then, interest has been low because of instability and a poor world copper price. The people brought in to help set up the mine have stayed on, settled down and now number 30,000.

Among them is a local Belgian family who bought the mine's surface assets in the 1980s and whose dispute over who owns them now is causing the concession's new holders maybe as great a headache as the rebels, still hundreds of miles away.

"We have kept water, electricity and roads working here and stopped the site being destroyed. We have saved TFM about five years of startup time," said entrepreneur Franz Couttenier, whose home sits in the middle of what will be mine headquarters.

Webb says the Coutteniers, who also run a railway car factory and Zaire's only model seed farm on the edge of the 74,000 acre concession, have a right to compensation, but must sort it out with Gecamines, which declined to comment.
He denies the family's suggestion that $50 million due to Gecamines for the mine deal has been withheld to force the bureaucratic, debt-ridden concern into solving the problem.
The money was due after the deal, giving Eurocan 55 percent of the joint venture, was signed in December. It had been put into a trust and Gecamines could take it any time, Webb said.
Meanwhile, the Couttenier family is staying put. The advance party of TFM security guards and geologists are learning to live with them as they start to transform the site.
Tenke has proven reserves of 222 million tons of ore, of which an average 4.4 percent will become pure copper and 0.33 percent precious cobalt, used in batteries and aviation.
Production is due to begin in early 2000 with an initial 100,000 tons of copper and 8,000 tons of cobalt a year, transforming the sleepy site into an enormous production line.
That is more than double all Zaire's current copper output and would meet a third of the annual world demand for cobalt.

The villagers of mud-hut Fungurume have rising hopes of jobs -- for many, the first formal employment in their lives -- and of a more prosperous future. But, having seen it all evaporate before, they have their fingers crossed.
